courseTitle: How IT Teams Work: Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban & Software Releases

slots.practicalActivity: Pick two real security initiatives and plan each under the model that actually fits it. First, a PCI-DSS compliance audit with a fixed scope and a regulator-set deadline: sketch it as a Waterfall plan with the 6 phases (Requirements, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, Maintenance), each given a fixed duration, the way the lesson's regulatory-report example argues for Waterfall. Second, a new employee phishing-simulation program whose content you expect to change as you see which emails people actually click: sketch it as 3 one-week Agile sprints, each with a one-sentence sprint goal. Write 2-3 sentences explaining why the audit belongs under Waterfall and the phishing program belongs under Agile.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written comparison showing a compliance audit planned under Waterfall's 6 phases and a phishing-simulation program planned under 3 Agile sprints, plus a short recommendation explaining why each initiative fits its model.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 4 user stories for a SOC backlog item in the "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]" shape — for example, "As a SOC analyst, I want failed-login alerts enriched with the source IP's threat-intel reputation, so that I can triage faster without pivoting to another tool." Give each story at least 2 specific, checkable acceptance criteria (not "it works" but something like "the enrichment data appears on the alert within 30 seconds of ingestion"). Then assign the three Scrum roles — Product Owner (the SOC manager), Scrum Master, Developers (the security engineers building the enrichment) — to yourself and two imaginary teammates, and write a 3-sentence Sprint Planning summary naming the sprint goal and which stories you'd pull into a one-week sprint.
slots.deliverable: 4 written SOC-backlog user stories with acceptance criteria, plus a short Sprint Planning summary naming the sprint goal and the stories committed to it.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a real Kanban board for a day's worth of SOC alert tickets, either on paper, in a spreadsheet, or in a free tool (Trello, GitHub Projects, or Jira's free tier) with columns Backlog, To Do (Triage), Investigating, Review, and Closed. Create 8-12 ticket cards representing a mix of alerts (a phishing report, a failed-login spike, a flagged outbound connection, a vulnerability-scan finding), set a WIP limit of 3 on "Investigating" the way an analyst would cap how many alerts they chase at once, and move at least 3 cards through two columns to simulate a shift of work. Mark one card "Blocked" with a one-sentence reason, such as waiting on a firewall-change approval before the investigation can continue.
slots.deliverable: A working Kanban board (screenshot or photo) with at least 8 alert-ticket cards distributed across its columns, a visible WIP limit on Investigating, and one card marked Blocked with a stated reason.

slots.practicalActivity: Trace a new SIEM detection rule (for example, one that flags impossible-travel logins) through Dev, QA, UAT, and Production exactly as the lesson's ticket-journey diagram lays it out: who writes and debugs the rule in Dev, what a teammate's code review would check before it merges, what a QA test plan would verify against sample log data (including a false-positive edge case, like a user legitimately traveling), what the SOC manager would check in UAT before trusting the rule, and what changes once it's live and firing real alerts in Production. Write one sentence for each environment naming the specific question it answers.
slots.deliverable: A written walkthrough of one detection rule through all 4 environments (Dev, QA, UAT, Production), with the owner and the specific question answered at each stage.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Git if needed, run git init to create a real local repository for a small "detection rules and playbooks" project, add a .gitignore that excludes anything resembling credentials or API keys, and make 3 real commits with specific messages (not "fixed stuff") as you add a README and two placeholder files representing a detection rule and an incident-response playbook. Create a branch named add-phishing-playbook, commit on it, then merge it back. If you have a GitHub account, push the repo and open a pull request for the branch before merging it there instead.
slots.deliverable: A real local (or GitHub) Git repository with a .gitignore, at least 3 commits with specific messages, and one branch that was created, committed to, and merged.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a release checklist for rolling out a new SIEM detection rule to production, covering all four required items: Approval (who signs off — the SOC manager or a change-advisory board), Monitoring (what you'd watch after release, like the rule's alert volume and false-positive rate), Rollback plan (the specific way to disable the rule if it floods the queue with noise), and Release notes (a real, specific note like the lesson's example, not "various improvements"). Then pick one deployment strategy (blue-green, canary, rolling, or feature flag) that fits rolling out a new detection rule and write 2-3 sentences justifying the choice — a canary release to a small log-source slice first is a natural fit here — over the other three.
slots.deliverable: A written release checklist (approval, monitoring, rollback plan, release notes) for one detection-rule release, plus a justified choice of deployment strategy.

slots.practicalActivity: Work through the full Castlebridge Retail capstone scenario from the lesson: write 3+ user stories (revenue-by-region, revenue-by-category, automatic refresh) with acceptance criteria, build a 5-column Kanban board and place the stories on it, write a short QA test plan including the zero-sales edge case, write a one-paragraph UAT sign-off in the sales director's voice, write a specific release note, and write how you'd investigate and communicate about the simulated production incident where a region shows zero sales two days after launch — as you investigate, note which logs or access records you'd check first to rule out a data or permissions problem, the same instinct you'll use chasing a real SOC alert.
slots.deliverable: A complete capstone packet: 3+ user stories with acceptance criteria, a Kanban board, a QA test plan with an edge case, a UAT sign-off, release notes, and a written incident-response plan for the zero-sales scenario.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can walk into any IT or security team's real workflow on day one — choosing between Agile and Waterfall for a given initiative, writing testable user stories for a SOC or engineering backlog, working a Kanban board for alert triage and ticket flow (including what a WIP limit and a Blocked card actually mean), tracing a change or detection rule through Dev/QA/UAT/Production, using Git's clone-branch-commit-push-pull-request cycle to version control real work like detection rules and playbooks, and reasoning through a CI/CD release checklist, a rollback plan, and a production incident end to end.
